name: Sky Network Television Limited
sector: Communication Services / Media & Entertainment (Pay-TV, Streaming, Broadcasting)
overview: Sky Network Television is New Zealand's dominant pay-TV, sports-rights aggregator and, since 1 August 2025, free-to-air broadcaster, operating a satellite pay-TV service (Sky Box), streaming products (Neon entertainment, Sky Sport Now, Sky Go), a small broadband ISP, a commercial/hospitality distribution business (Sky Business), and, following the near-nil-cost acquisition of Discovery NZ (renamed Sky Free), the free-to-air channels Three/Eden/Rush/HGTV and the ThreeNow BVOD streaming platform. The core business is built around exclusive New Zealand and international sports rights (All Blacks/Super Rugby, NZ Cricket, NRL, EPL, Formula 1, PGA Tour, Olympics) monetised across a linear satellite base in structural decline and a growing streaming/digital/advertising base. Revenue was NZ$750.7m (reported) / $755.1m (adjusted) in FY2025, growing to underlying $826.1m in FY2026 (+9%), with underlying EBITDA of $157m (+6%) for FY2026; the company holds a net cash balance sheet and pays a growing fully-imputed dividend (32 cps declared for FY2026).

business_model.summary: Sky earns subscription revenue from three delivery platforms carrying largely the same premium sport/entertainment content library (satellite Sky Box, streaming Neon/Sky Sport Now, and now free-to-air Three/ThreeNow), plus advertising sold across linear FTA, pay-TV, and digital inventory, a small broadband ISP, and commercial/hospitality distribution (Sky Business, ~6,000 premises). Historically almost entirely subscription-funded, the Discovery NZ acquisition materially increases the advertising revenue mix and gives Sky a genuinely 'free' consumer proposition for the first time, diversifying away from a satellite base that has been shrinking for a decade. Content is largely 'pass-through' from global studios/sports bodies but is increasingly supplemented with locally commissioned Sky NZ Originals content.

revenue_streams.name: Sky Box (satellite pay-TV subscriptions)
revenue_streams.note: $465.5m of $750.7m FY2025 revenue (62% of FY25 revenue per CEO letter, ~54-62% depending on basis); Sky Box customers fell from 514,982 (FY2023) to ~435,000 (H1 FY2026), a rate of roughly 5-8% p.a.

revenue_streams.name: Streaming subscriptions (Neon, Sky Sport Now, Sky Go)
revenue_streams.note: $118.8m FY2025; Sky Sport Now growing (170,000 customers, digital streams +15% in FY25) while Neon entertainment streaming fell 17% in H1 FY2026 to 215,000 customers on thin content slate and non-renewal of exclusive HBO Max

revenue_streams.name: Advertising (linear + digital)
revenue_streams.note: $57.1m FY2025 (+7% YoY) rising to $64.1m in H1 FY2026 alone (+114% YoY) after Sky Free consolidation; digital advertising still small ($5.1m FY2025, 9% of ad revenue) but the primary strategic growth lever post-acquisition

revenue_streams.name: Sky Free (Three, Eden, Rush, HGTV, ThreeNow) - post 1 Aug 2025
revenue_streams.note: Contributed $35.6m revenue and a modest $0.4m pre-tax profit in its first 5 months (Aug-Dec 2025); estimated $42.7m on a pro-rata 6-month basis; largely an advertising-funded FTA/BVOD business bolted onto Sky's subscription base

revenue_streams.name: Broadband subscriptions
revenue_streams.note: $37.0m FY2025 (+34% YoY) off a small base; over 50,000 customers at FY2025 year end; small but fast-growing bundling/retention tool

business_model.customer_type: B2C mass-market residential (satellite, streaming, broadband, FTA) plus B2B commercial/hospitality (Sky Business) and B2B advertisers/sponsors
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand (Aotearoa NZ-focused strategy); NZD functional currency but material USD/AUD content and capex exposure (studios, sports rights, satellite)

main_competitors: Warner Bros. Discovery (former content partner, now also a direct competitor)
NZME/Stuff (advertising, and news bargaining bill counterparties)
competitive_position.market_position: Still New Zealand's largest aggregator of premium sport and pay entertainment, and, since August 2025, also owns a top-3 free-to-air network (Three) and BVOD platform (ThreeNow), giving it reach across virtually every screen and price point in the country; company states it reaches 'over 1 in 3 New Zealanders each month' across its multi-platform services (FY2023 disclosure).

moat_factors.description: Long-dated exclusive deals for All Blacks/Black Ferns/Super Rugby (NZR, 2026-2030), NZ Cricket (6-year deal from 2026-27), NRL, EPL (through 2027-28), Formula 1, PGA Tour/Olympics (through Brisbane 2032), Six Nations/Premiership Rugby (8-year deal). This content is largely unavailable elsewhere in NZ and is the primary reason satellite/streaming customers pay.
Only provider with 100% satellite coverage of NZ combined with streaming and, now, free-to-air; useful for both content partners negotiating maximum audience and advertisers wanting full-funnel reach

Sky Sales won 'Sales Team of the Year' 2025; independent measurement showed Sky's linear TV ad revenue share rose to 14% (+11%) even as the total linear market fell 11%; Discovery NZ acquisition materially scales this business and its data/DAI (dynamic ad insertion) capability

Net cash position ($99.9m cash at 31 Dec 2025, $100m undrawn facility, no net debt), unlike most global streamers still burning cash; allows Sky to out-compete DAZN/others on rational, disciplined rights bidding

35+ year history as NZ's default sport/entertainment aggregator, but brand increasingly associated with legacy satellite technology and past price increases/customer service issues (2025 satellite migration disruption)

weaknesses: No content ownership at scale — Sky is fundamentally a rights aggregator/reseller dependent on renewing expensive contracts with NZR, NZC, NRL, WBD, BBC, Paramount etc., each a renewal/repricing risk

Satellite technology is structurally obsolete versus IP-delivered global streaming, requiring costly hardware (Sky Box/Pod), field technicians, and a fragile single-satellite dependency (evidenced by the disruptive 2025 Optus D2-to-KT6 migration)
Small absolute scale (NZ-only, ~5m population) versus global streamers' content budgets amortised across hundreds of millions of subscribers
Newly acquired Sky Free/Three was a loss-making, declining, indebted business under Warner Bros. Discovery ownership for years — turnaround/synergy delivery is unproven
Linear TV advertising market itself is shrinking (total market -11% in FY25) even as Sky gains share within it

growth_drivers: Discovery NZ/Sky Free integration: management targets at least $10m incremental EBITDA by FY28 from cost synergies (already $3.2m delivered by H1 FY26) plus revenue synergies across advertising and digital; FY27 is explicitly flagged as the year growth is expected to 'accelerate' post-integration

Advertising diversification: digital advertising climbing from a low base ($5.1m FY25, 9% of ad revenue) with new DAI (dynamic ad insertion) technology on Sky Sport Now and now a scaled FTA/BVOD sales inventory via Three/ThreeNow
Broadband cross-sell: fast-growing but small (50,000+ customers, +34% revenue FY25) via fibre company partnerships and bundling, a retention tool against Spark/One NZ
New Sky Experience (IP-hybrid Sky Box/Pod) migration: 37% of base converted by FY25 (from 21%), improving reliability (IP failover) and reducing churn/discounting

Content rights renewals secured on improved economics: the reset NZR deal (2026-2030, ~$75-80m/yr vs prior ~$111m/yr) plus new NZ Cricket, Six Nations/Premiership Rugby, PGA Tour and extended Olympic rights (to Brisbane 2032) lock in the core sports moat at a lower/more sustainable cost base, supporting management's target of holding programming costs at 47-49% of revenue
Continued dividend growth / capital return optionality once integration synergies are delivered and the balance sheet is reviewed (see Capital Returns below)

business.description: Sky Box customers fell from 514,982 (FY2023) to ~448,000 (FY2025) to ~435,000 (H1 FY2026); satellite still ~54-62% of group revenue depending on measure, and once IP-delivered content becomes materially cheaper/more available, this remains a shrinking, high-cost-to-serve legacy base

Neon fell 17% in H1 FY2026 to 215,000 customers, driven by a thin content slate and the disciplined decision not to renew exclusive HBO Max (which launches standalone in NZ from 16 June 2026) — Sky's own streaming arm is now shrinking, not just satellite

The single largest content cost and revenue anchor is NZ Rugby. NZR reportedly explored DAZN as an alternative before renewing with Sky in 2025 at a materially reduced ~30% lower annual fee (~$75-80m vs ~$111m) and on a co-exclusive (not fully exclusive) basis with TVNZ taking provincial rugby FTA — evidence both that Sky needed to cut a cheaper deal to retain the rights and that NZR is willing to fragment exclusivity. Any future loss of All Blacks/Super Rugby rights to a global streamer (Amazon, DAZN) would be an existential risk to the subscription base

business.risk: Sky Free/Discovery NZ integration and turnaround risk
business.description: Board's own strategic risk disclosure flags 'failure to successfully decouple from Warner Bros. Discovery and integrate Sky Free' as a top risk; the acquired business had a history of losses and growing indebtedness under WBD ownership; technology/team integration is complex and ongoing through FY26/27
The accelerated 2025 Optus D2-to-KoreaSat6 migration caused significant customer disruption (500+ service callouts/day at peak) and reputational damage, illustrating single-satellite dependency risk

financial.description: Sky hedges USD/AUD exposure on programming rights, capex and lease costs via forward FX contracts (per FY2026 interim notes), but a weaker NZD raises effective content costs against the 47-49%-of-revenue target

The $34.4m gain on bargain purchase (Discovery NZ) and the Optus compensation ($8.2m) inflate FY2026 H1 statutory NPAT ($52.4m) well above underlying profit ($19.3m); investors reading headline statutory EPS (37.9 cents H1) without adjusting will overstate run-rate earnings power

regulatory.description: Government progressing a revised (Australian-style, ministerial-designation) news bargaining code aimed at Google/Meta paying NZ news publishers; likely benefits TVNZ/NZME more directly than Sky, which does not operate an independent newsroom, but the acquired Three/ThreeNow FTA business brings Sky more directly into NZ media-policy discussions and local-content-quota debates

Sky content is regulated under both the Broadcasting Standards Code and Commercial Video on Demand Code; no BSA complaints referred in FY25, but the expanded FTA footprint increases regulatory surface area

NZ Takeovers Code, Overseas Investment Act and Commerce Act apply; ACC (10.6%) and NZ Super Fund (7.4%) are large disclosed holders as at mid-2025, alongside historic NZR shareholding (1.3%) from the prior rights deal structure

macro.risk: NZ recession / weak consumer and ad spend
macro.description: Management has repeatedly cited 'tough economic conditions,' worse-than-forecast NZ economic weakness, and 'subdued consumer and corporate spend' adversely impacting both subscription and advertising revenue through FY24-FY26; discretionary subscription products (Sky Box, Neon) are directly exposed to household budget pressure and churn/downgrade risk in a downturn

Total NZ linear TV advertising market fell -11% in FY25 even as Sky grew share; the newly acquired Sky Free free-to-air business is a bet that Sky can outperform a shrinking linear ad pool via digital/BVOD growth

macro.risk: Global content cost inflation / streamer consolidation
macro.description: Global SVOD players raising prices and consolidating (per Sky's own FY24 chairman's letter) as they seek profitability, which could flow through to higher content costs for Sky as a licensee, or alternatively benefit Sky if it drives rational pricing/bundling behaviour

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global pay-TV in structural decline as IP/streaming displaces satellite/cable; NZ market specifically has seen Spark Sport exit live sports streaming (ceding rights back to the market, some picked up by Sky), TVNZ+ scale as the free BVOD leader, and international SVOD (Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime, and now standalone HBO Max from June 2026) directly compete for entertainment subscription dollars. Sky's strategic response — becoming a genuine multi-platform (satellite + streaming + FTA + broadband) aggregator via the Discovery NZ acquisition — is a direct bet that bundled reach and locally-exclusive sports content can offset secular decline in any single platform.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderately cyclical — subscription and advertising revenue both correlate with NZ consumer/business confidence and discretionary spend; company has explicitly cited the 2023-2026 NZ recession/weak-economy period as a persistent headwind to both revenue lines
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct balance-sheet sensitivity given net cash position and undrawn $100m facility; moderate indirect sensitivity via NZ consumer discretionary spending and housing-linked household budgets
key_input_costs: Sports and content broadcasting rights (NZR, NZC, NRL, EPL, F1, PGA Tour, WBD/HBO, BBC, Paramount)
Subscriber equipment (Sky Box/Pod hardware) and installation

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results released: underlying revenue $826.1m (+9%), underlying EBITDA $157m (+6%), statutory NPAT $59.8m (vs $20.6m FY2025) boosted by the ~$34m Discovery NZ bargain-purchase gain and Optus compensation; underlying NPAT $41.8m (+2%); full-year dividend of 32 cps declared, above the 'at least 30 cps' guidance

Warner Bros. Discovery launched HBO Max as a standalone streaming service in New Zealand, following Sky's decision not to renew exclusive HBO Max distribution rights beyond June 2026 — a direct new competitor to Neon

H1 FY2026 interim results: underlying revenue $415.4m (+8%), underlying EBITDA $78.2m (+29%), underlying NPAT $19.3m (+77%); statutory NPAT $52.4m including $34.4m bargain-purchase gain and $8.2m Optus satellite-migration compensation; interim dividend of 15.0 cps (+76.5% YoY); FY26 guidance narrowed to revenue $820-835m, EBITDA $145-160m, capex $62-68m, dividend at least 30 cps; Sky Box customers down to ~435,000, Neon down 17% to 215,000, Sky Sport Now up to 170,000

Completed acquisition of Discovery NZ Limited (Three, Eden, Rush, HGTV, ThreeNow) from Warner Bros. Discovery for nominal consideration ($1 share price) on a debt-free, working-capital-adjusted basis, resulting in a $34.4m accounting gain on bargain purchase; renamed Sky Free

Announced new 5-year (2026-2030) NZ Rugby/SANZAAR broadcast rights deal, reportedly worth NZ$75-80m per year versus ~NZ$111m/year previously — roughly a 30% cost reduction — retaining exclusive All Blacks/Black Ferns/Super Rugby/Bledisloe Cup/Rugby Championship/British & Irish Lions rights, while TVNZ becomes the free-to-air partner for provincial rugby (National Provincial Championship, Farah Palmer Cup)

Completed accelerated 'Project Migrate' satellite transition from the end-of-life Optus D2 satellite to KoreaSat6, following disruption and service issues for some customers in the lead-up; received subsequent compensation from Optus

Board paused the on-market share buyback (initially due to NZR negotiations, then due to the DNZ acquisition) and stated capital management options would be reviewed following successful integration of Sky Free, to be updated at the FY26 annual results

Reported revenue $750.7m (adjusted $755.1m, slightly down YoY), reported EBITDA $120.6m (adjusted $148.5m), final dividend 13.5 cps taking full-year dividend to 22 cps (+15.8% YoY); results at the lower end of revised guidance given in February 2025, reflecting weak economy and satellite-migration disruption

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Results / H1 FY2026 Interim Report (25 February 2026)

items.notes: H1 FY26 guidance narrowed the prior range as Group guidance (first time including Sky Free on a full-guidance basis) after five months of Sky Free contribution

Achieved near the top of the range; management flagged 'modest forecast EBITDA growth' in FY26 due to reinvestment in marketing/CX/people and a muted first-half impact of the new, cheaper NZR deal given phasing of the final year of payments under the old deal
Down from the elevated satellite-migration-affected FY24/FY25 capex intensity target of 7-9% of revenue (adjusted to exclude migration spend)
Part of a 3-year target (announced FY24) to double the dividend to 30 cps by FY26 — achieved a year ahead of / in line with plan; FY23 15 cps -> FY24 19 cps -> FY25 22 cps -> FY26 32 cps
FY25 actual was 50.9% (still above target, 'likely to be at the lower end' per FY25 report); new, cheaper NZR deal (~30% lower annual cost) is explicitly designed to help hit this target from FY26/27
FY25 actual 19.7% (Year 2 of 3), flagged as 'likely to be at the lower end of the range'
$3.2m of synergies already delivered by H1 FY26; further savings expected from transitioning services away from Warner Bros. Discovery and harmonising systems/teams

items.vs_prior: new framing introduced with Sky Free acquisition
items.notes: Management explicitly frames FY26 as an integration year, with FY27 the year growth is expected to 'accelerate' as Sky Free synergies, advertising growth and the reset NZR economics come through

As at H1 FY26, management said it 'will review capital management options following the successful integration of Sky Free and update shareholders on any new initiatives as part of the Annual Results announcement' (i.e., the 28 August 2026 FY26 result)

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Sophie Moloney: FY26 priorities are 'Successful Integration' of Sky Free, 'Deepen content engagement,' 'Supercharge new Sky Experience,' and 'Accelerate advertising,' explicitly positioned as underpinning 'Accelerating our growth from FY27.' Management has repeatedly flagged 'trading conditions remain challenging in the near term' given the weak NZ economy, softer-than-expected linear advertising, and continuing satellite/streaming subscriber attrition, while expressing confidence in the strategic and financial rationale for the Discovery NZ acquisition and reaffirming the at-least-$10m FY28 synergy target and at-least-30cps FY26 dividend (both subsequently delivered/beaten).

bull_case: Net-cash balance sheet with a fully imputed, fast-growing dividend (15 cps in FY23 to 32 cps in FY26, more than doubled in three years) makes this a credible income/yield stock (implied yield roughly 9-10% on a ~$3.30-3.40 share price) even before any capital-management upside from a resumed buyback

The Discovery NZ acquisition was effectively free (nominal $1 consideration, debt-free, cash-positive on completion) and immediately diversifies revenue into advertising/digital and a genuine free-to-air/BVOD offering, with disclosed synergy targets ($10m+ EBITDA by FY28) that management is already ahead of schedule on ($3.2m delivered in H1 FY26 alone)

The reset NZ Rugby deal (2026-2030, ~$75-80m/yr vs ~$111m/yr) materially de-risks the single largest content cost line while still retaining the exclusive core rugby product, directly supporting the 47-49% programming-cost-to-revenue target and structural margin improvement

Sports rights moat remains intact and recently extended across multiple codes (NZ Cricket 6-year deal, EPL to 2027-28, Olympics to Brisbane 2032, Six Nations/Premiership 8-year deal), evidencing continued ability to secure/retain exclusive premium content that global generalist streamers have shown limited appetite to contest in a small market

FY2026 results (revenue +9%, EBITDA +6%, dividend beat at 32 cps) demonstrate the business can grow through a weak NZ economy and a major technology transition, with management explicitly guiding to accelerating growth from FY27 as integration synergies land
bear_case: The core satellite subscriber base continues to shrink every reporting period (Sky Box customers down from ~515,000 in FY23 to ~435,000 in H1 FY26) and Neon streaming, which was supposed to be the replacement growth engine, has now also gone into reverse (-17% in H1 FY26) following the loss of exclusive HBO Max — the 'offset the decline' thesis is not yet proven in the data

Sky Free/Discovery NZ was a loss-making, indebted business for years under sophisticated global-media ownership (Warner Bros. Discovery); turning around a structurally declining linear FTA advertising business (total NZ linear ad market -11% in FY25) while simultaneously executing a complex technology/team integration carries real execution risk

NZ Rugby is a single point of failure for the whole content strategy; the fact that NZR needed to be retained at a ~30% lower price and with reduced (non-provincial) exclusivity shows Sky's negotiating leverage has weakened, and a future move by a well-capitalised global streamer (Amazon, DAZN) for all-or-part of the rights bundle remains a real long-term tail risk

Heavy reliance on discretionary household and business spending in a New Zealand economy management itself has repeatedly described as recessionary/challenging for three consecutive years, with no clear inflection point yet visible in subscriber or linear-ad trends

Statutory FY2026 profit growth is flattered by one-off, non-cash and non-recurring items (bargain-purchase gain, Optus compensation); underlying NPAT growth of just 2% for FY26 is a much more modest true earnings trajectory than the headline statutory profit-near-tripling figures suggest, and the capital-management/buyback resumption remains only a stated intention pending integration proof-points
